newsitem.title: DENMARK: Danish police warily welcome biker truce offer.
newsitem.headline: Danish police warily welcome biker truce offer.

text.p: The leader of Denmark's Bandidos motorcycle gang, locked in a bloody war with the rival Hell's Angels for almost three years, has offered a truce, saying the war risked harming innocent people.
"We want it stopped, because it is hurting many innocent biker clubs and can hurt many innocent people, as well," Bandidos President Jim Tinndahn told Danish state television on Thursday.
Police gave the offer a cautious welcome but said they were not sure if he spoke for all his members or their allies.

Tinndahn denied knowing who carried out an October 6 missile attack on Hell's Angels' Copenhagen headquarters, which killed two people, wounded 19 and stiffened the government's resolve to stop the bloodshed.
He suggested that a spate of bomb, grenade, machine gun and rocket attacks on Hell's Angels' strongholds were the work of rogue bikers not under his orders.
"The Bandidos think this has gone too far and are trying to send a message to those on the fringe, who we do not exactly have control over, who are doing these things," he said.
Hell's Angels' occasional spokesman Joenke Nielsen refused to comment on the offer.
Detective Chief Inspector Per Larsen, a leader of the Danish police anti-biker task force, welcomed the proposal, but was unsure if it could be made to hold.
"If we can believe what Tinndahn says here then it is certainly good news. What worries me is if he is in control of all of his troops," he told the television.
"He speaks of those on the periphery and it is perhaps from there that some of this plague comes from," Larsen said.

The two gangs, both offshoots of U.S. groups, have been fighting a bloody turf war across the Nordic region almost since the Bandidos set up shop here in late 1993. Seven people have died since, in Denmark, Finland, Norway and Sweden.
It was not immediately clear if Tinndahn was also proposing a truce on behalf of Bandidos in the other Nordic countries.

Tinndahn appeared to offer to turn in his gang's arms -- which judging from attacks on Hell's Angels include military machine guns, hand grenades and anti-tank missiles -- if Hell's Angels would do the same.

"Sure we're willling to deliver our weapons in the event of peace, but what kind of peace ? Those who have weapons have them to defend themselves. The day that they no longer need to defend themselves they also don't need weapons," he said.

The peace initiative came just one day after a new Danish law suspending bikers' right of assembly and driving them from their fortified clubhouses took effect, with the promise of still tougher sanctions and possibly a total ban yet to come.

In an interview on Wednesday Danish journalist Ambro Kragh, who has covered this and other biker feuds for the past six years, predicted that the government offensive would force the bikers to proclaim peace, to avert a clampdown that could finish them both.

"As the so-called one percent of motorcyclists who are criminals, they have a sense of brotherhood among themselves and I believe they are going to meet and say: 'Look, we are going to be killed by the politicians if we continue (fighting)'," Kragh told Reuters.
